headline_marked: [[AI agent fully routes complex Raspberry Pi CM4 IO board]], but a critical power fault blocks manufacturing
headline: AI agent fully routes complex Raspberry Pi CM4 IO board, but a critical power fault blocks manufacturing
summary: An AI agent successfully routed a Raspberry Pi CM4 Mini-ITX IO board with zero unrouted nets, yet a fault simulation reveals a persistent -1.35V issue on a power controller pin, preventing manufacturability.
details: An AI agent, Codex, successfully completed the routing of a complex Raspberry Pi CM4 Mini-ITX IO board. The design achieved perfect scores with zero unrouted nets, ERC errors, DRC errors, or schematic-to-PCB mismatches.

Despite this routing success, the board is still not deemed manufacturable due to a critical issue identified during fault simulation. A power controller pin shows a persistent -1.35V, falling below the acceptable check floor of -0.3V.

Vendor-model power simulations for all 12 cases (covering startup, output short circuit, and normal input loss for four power branches) now complete successfully within 300 ms. These simulations passed limited terminal-voltage and MOSFET-voltage checks against saved waveforms.

An internal-fault diagnosis points to a 1 mΩ short on the upstream BUCK side as the cause of the voltage anomaly. Proposed solutions, including added capacitors and snubbers, failed to resolve the issue and were not incorporated into the design.

The design remains incomplete, problem-free, and unmanufacturable until this specific fault is fully resolved and explained. While the model is partial and might not perfectly reflect a real board, "the model might be wrong" is not an acceptable passing grade.

Further stages of verification are still pending, including comprehensive fault tolerance analysis, the full power control loop, high-speed signal integrity, thermal and EMI considerations, and real-world I/O checks. Case, assembly, and manufacturing checks also remain.

The board's specifications include DisplayPort and HDMI outputs, two USB-A ports, two USB-C ports, and a PCIe switch feeding two slots and two M.2 connectors. It is powered by an ATX 24-pin connector.

headline_marked: [[Meta's crawler goes live Oct 30]], but your real robots.txt deadline is Oct 29.
headline: Meta's crawler goes live Oct 30, but your real robots.txt deadline is Oct 29.
summary: Meta's updated Commercial Terms allow it to crawl associated websites for training purposes starting October 30, 2026. However, robots.txt changes can take up to 24 hours to propagate, making October 29 the effective last day for safe edits.
details: Meta's updated Commercial Terms authorize it to crawl websites associated with business accounts for product training, effective October 30, 2026. However, any changes to your robots.txt file can take up to 24 hours to propagate across the web. This effectively moves the real deadline for safe edits to October 29.

Many sites risk being surprised by mismatches between their intended robots.txt rules and what crawlers actually receive. Common issues include staging/production drift, CDN caching of old files, and server-side rules overriding robots.txt directives.

A study of top 1,000 sites found 8-11% of servers refused AI crawlers despite robots.txt explicitly allowing them, due to bot-management rules or firewalls. Cloudflare's retirement of its "Block AI Bots" toggle also silently removed bans for 118 sites.

Outdated robots.txt snippets, often copied from pre-answer-crawler distinctions, can inadvertently block user-initiated fetching alongside training. This can break "summarize this URL" features for ChatGPT users and cause unexplained traffic dips.

It's crucial to distinguish between blocking training crawlers (like GPTBot) and allowing answer crawlers (like OAI-SearchBot or ChatGPT-User) based on purpose, not just company logo. Incorrect rules can negatively impact user experience and site visibility.

To verify compliance, fetch your live robots.txt file, not just the repo copy, to ensure it's what the internet sees. Establish per-purpose rules, run verification checks, and save a log baseline for future audits.

The clause is a contractual change, making crawler hygiene a critical, one-evening job. The verification process is more important than the rules themselves, as many sites fail to confirm what their live robots.txt actually serves.
